title: Hydrolea zeylanica: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Hydrolea zeylanica in Rice: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Hydrolea zeylanica can cut transplanted rice yield by up to 52 percent. Learn to spot its creeping stems and blue flowers, and stop it spreading.
excerpt: Hydrolea zeylanica is a creeping broadleaf weed with blue purple flowers. Farmers call it kangkong kangkungan or lupo lupo. It grows in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines, and it spreads fast under flooding. This page shows you how to spot it and how much harvest it can take. It also shows how to control it before it takes over.

blocks.text:
Hydrolea zeylanica is a creeping herb that likes wet ground. In English it is called Ceylon hydrolea. Farmers know it as kangkong kangkungan, garampingat or lupo lupo. Its hollow stems crawl along the soil while the tips turn upward. It is a broadleaf weed, not a grass or sedge, and it belongs to the Hydrophyllaceae family.

You will find it in irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields. Most plants live on from season to season, though some last only one season. It spreads in two ways. First, its creeping stems act as runners and set down new plants. Next, it also makes seeds. Even cut pieces of stem can grow into new plants. So weeding that leaves broken stems in the mud can spread it further.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Hydrolea zeylanica
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Look for hollow stems creeping flat on the mud, with the tips curving upward. The leaves are lance shaped to oval, pointed at both the base and the tip, with smooth edges. Some plants have smooth leaves, while others have fine hairs. Like other broadleaf weeds, the leaves have netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. When it flowers, look for bright blue purple petals near the stem tips.

items: Hollow stems lying flat on the mud, with the growing tips turning upward.
Lance shaped to oval leaves, pointed at both ends, with smooth edges.
Leaves that are either smooth or covered with fine hairs, from plant to plant.
Blue purple flowers near the stem tips, easy to see against green rice.
New plants springing up where broken stem pieces were left in flooded mud.

blocks.text:
This weed takes hold fast. Even a cut piece of stem can sprout into a new plant, so it fills a field quickly, most of all when the paddy is flooded. In fact, the standing water that holds back many other weeds does not stop this one.

If you leave it alone, it can take a big share of your harvest. In transplanted rice, it can cut grain yield by as much as 52 percent. In wet direct seeded rice, the loss can reach 6 percent. Those numbers come from fields where the weed was not controlled. So early action protects the most palay, especially in transplanted fields where the loss runs highest.

items: When you hand weed, pull out the whole plant and carry every stem piece out of the paddy. Cut pieces left in the mud can grow again.
Do not just chop it into the mud with a rotary weeder. Broken stems can spread the weed instead of killing it.
Start weeding early in transplanted fields, where the yield loss can be highest. Do not wait for the blue flowers to show.
Check the bunds and canal edges, since creeping stems there can crawl back into the field.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Hydrolea zeylanica down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Hydrolea zeylanica Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Hydrolea zeylanica?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Hydrolea zeylanica

items.q: What is Hydrolea zeylanica called in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers call it kangkong kangkungan, garampingat or lupo lupo, depending on the place. In English it is called Ceylon hydrolea. The name kangkong kangkungan means something like false kangkong, but it is a different plant from the kangkong we cook. Treat it as a weed whenever it shows up in your palay.

items.q: How do I control kangkong kangkungan in my rice field?
items.a: Start with thorough land preparation and clean seed. Hand weed early, pull the whole plant, and take every stem piece out of the field, since cut stems can regrow. Flooding alone will not stop it. If you need a herbicide, choose one for broadleaf weeds that matches the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it spread after I weed it?
items.a: Cut stems of this weed can grow into new plants. If you chop it and leave the pieces in wet mud, each piece may start a new plant. That is why a quick weeding can make the patch bigger. Pull whole plants, gather the broken pieces, and dry them on high ground away from the paddy.
